symbols.name: K
symbols.def: A fixed number of arms that does not vary with \(n\).

symbols.name: \mathcal A_K
symbols.def: \(\mathcal A_K=\{1,\ldots,K\}\).

symbols.name: n
symbols.def: Number of experimental units.

symbols.name: i
symbols.def: Generic unit label.

symbols.name: a
symbols.def: Generic treatment-arm label.

symbols.name: c
symbols.def: Fixed coefficient vector \(c=(c_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\).

symbols.name: S_c
symbols.def: \(S_c=\{a\in\mathcal A_K:c_a\ne0\}\).

symbols.name: L_c
symbols.def: \(L_c=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|c_a|\).

symbols.name: q^\star
symbols.def: \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) for \(a\in S_c\) and \(q_a^\star=0\) otherwise.

symbols.name: t
symbols.def: Generic vector \(t=(t_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\) of arm-specific binary potential outcomes.

symbols.name: \mathcal T_K
symbols.def: \(\mathcal T_K=\{0,1\}^{\mathcal A_K}\), with \(|\mathcal T_K|=2^K\).

symbols.name: z
symbols.def: \(z=(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\), where each labeled unit response type \(t_i=(t_{i,a})_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\) belongs to \(\mathcal T_K\).

symbols.name: Y_i(a)
symbols.def: \(Y_i(a)=t_{i,a}\), the arm \(a\) coordinate of unit \(i\)'s response type in \(z\).

symbols.name: A
symbols.def: \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is drawn from a design selected before the fixed potential outcomes are revealed.

symbols.name: \mathcal D
symbols.def: Probability law of \(A\), chosen without knowledge of the response schedule.

symbols.name: Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
symbols.def: \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(A_i)\).

symbols.name: \tau_c(z)
symbols.def: \(\tau_c(z)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_{i,a}\).

symbols.name: \widehat\tau
symbols.def: Any measurable, possibly biased function of \((A_i,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})_{i=1}^n\), clipped to the range of \(\tau_c(z)\).

symbols.name: R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)
symbols.def: \(R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[(\widehat\tau-\tau_c(z))^2]\), where the expectation is only over assignment from \(\mathcal D\).

symbols.name: \rho_n(c)
symbols.def: \(\rho_n(c)=\inf_{\mathcal D,\widehat\tau}\max_{z\in\mathcal T_K^n}R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau;z)\).

symbols.name: m
symbols.def: For a labeled schedule \(z\), \(m=(m_t)_{t\in\mathcal T_K}\) is its unit-permutation orbit, with \(m_t=\#\{i:t_i=t\}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal M_{n,K}
symbols.def: \(\mathcal M_{n,K}=\{m\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal T_K}:\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_K}m_t=n\}\).

symbols.name: \tau_c(m)
symbols.type: orbit form of the causal contrast
symbols.def: \(\tau_c(m)=n^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_K}m_t\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_a\).

symbols.name: r
symbols.def: \(r=(r_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\), where \(r_a=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal R_{n,K}
symbols.def: \(\mathcal R_{n,K}=\{r\in\mathbb Z_+^{\mathcal A_K}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}r_a=n\}\).

symbols.name: x
symbols.def: \(x=(x_a)_{a\in\mathcal A_K}\), where \(x_a=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{A_i=a,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=1\}\).

symbols.name: h
symbols.def: \(h=(h_{t,a})\) records how many units of response type \(t\) are assigned arm \(a\).

symbols.name: \mathcal H(m,r,x)
symbols.def: The set of \(h\) satisfying \(\sum_a h_{t,a}=m_t\), \(\sum_t h_{t,a}=r_a\), and \(\sum_{t:t_a=1}h_{t,a}=x_a\) for every \(t\) and \(a\).

symbols.name: P_m(x\mid r)
symbols.def: Probability of observed success counts \(x\) under uniform assignment conditional on allocation counts \(r\) and response-type counts \(m\).

symbols.name: \pi
symbols.def: \(\pi=(\pi_r)_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}}\) selects an allocation count and then assigns units uniformly conditional on that count.

symbols.name: \delta
symbols.def: Deterministic estimator based only on the allocation and observed-success orbits \((r,x)\).

symbols.name: G_n(c)
symbols.def: Minimax value of the explicit orbit experiment over \(\pi\), \(\delta\), and \(m\).

symbols.name: p_+
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(p_+=m_{(1,0)}\).

symbols.name: p_-
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(p_-=m_{(0,1)}\).

symbols.name: r_0
symbols.def: Parameter of the published two-arm scalar experiment; when related to the full four-count orbit vector, \(r_0=m_{(0,0)}+m_{(1,1)}\), with \(p_++p_-+r_0=n\). This aggregation does not replace the separate counts \(m_{(0,0)}\) and \(m_{(1,1)}\) in the orbit likelihood.

symbols.name: X_2
symbols.def: The scalar observation \(X_2=p_++\operatorname{Binomial}(r_0,1/2)\) in the published two-arm reduced experiment.

symbols.name: C_A
symbols.def: The published scalar Airy ground-state constant \(C_A=1.617\ldots\).

symbols.name: \widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star
symbols.def: Under independent assignment supported on \(S_c\) with probabilities \(q^\star\), \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star=\operatorname{proj}_{[-L_c/2,L_c/2]}\!\left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1/2)/q_a^\star\right]\).

symbols.name: a_n
symbols.def: A deterministic positive sequence indexed by \(n\).

symbols.name: C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)
symbols.def: Conditional on the branch in which a normalizer \(a_n\) exists and \(a_nd_n(c)\) converges to a finite positive limit, \(C_{\mathrm{so}}(c)=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_nd_n(c)\).

symbols.name: \sigma
symbols.def: A generic bijection of the arm index set.

symbols.name: \mathfrak G_c
symbols.def: \(\mathfrak G_c=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal A_K):\exists s\in\{-1,1\},\ c_{\sigma(a)}=s c_a\text{ for every }a\in\mathcal A_K\}\).

symbols.name: \rho_n^\dagger
symbols.def: \(\rho_n^\dagger=\rho_n(c^\dagger)\), for which \(C_0(c^\dagger)=1\).

symbols.name: M
symbols.def: Positive integer controlling the mesh of the rational action grid.

symbols.name: j
symbols.def: Generic integer index for the rational action grid.

symbols.name: g
symbols.def: Generic estimator action in the rational grid.

symbols.name: u
symbols.def: Upper bound on every response-type risk in the grid-action LP.

symbols.name: w_{r,x,g}
symbols.def: Nonnegative joint weight for allocation orbit \(r\), observation orbit \(x\), and randomized grid action \(g\).

symbols.name: \Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger
symbols.def: Value of the finite rational linear program that uses the exact three-arm orbit likelihood and permits randomized estimator actions in \(\Gamma_M\).

symbols.name: \Gamma_{M,c}
symbols.def: For a rational nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\), put \(h_c=L_c/2\) and \(\Gamma_{M,c}=\{-h_c+jh_c/M:j=0,\ldots,2M\}\).

symbols.name: \Lambda_{n,M}(c)
symbols.def: Value of the finite exact-rational grid-action linear program for contrast \(c\) on \(\Gamma_{M,c}\).

definitions.name: Signed contrast stabilizer
definitions.construction: \[\mathfrak G_c=\left\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\mathcal A_K):\exists s\in\{-1,1\}\text{ such that }c_{\sigma(a)}=s c_a\text{ for all }a\in\mathcal A_K\right\}.\]

definitions.name: Contrast-weighted first-order procedure
definitions.construction: Assign each \(A_i\) independently on \(S_c\) with \(\Pr(A_i=a)=q_a^\star\), and report \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star=\operatorname{proj}_{[-L_c/2,L_c/2]}\!\left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1/2)/q_a^\star\right]\).

definitions.name: Three-arm exact-rational grid-action LP
definitions.construction: For \(K=3\) and \(c=c^\dagger\), minimize \(u\) over rational variables \(\pi_r\ge0\) and \(w_{r,x,g}\ge0\), subject to \(\sum_r\pi_r=1\), \(\sum_{g\in\Gamma_M}w_{r,x,g}=\pi_r\) for every \((r,x)\), and \(\sum_{r,x,g}P_m(x\mid r)w_{r,x,g}\{g-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2\le u\) for every \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,3}\); its value is \(\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\).

definitions.name: Active-face boundary-layer handle
definitions.construction: Starting from the exact orbit game, enumerate binding response-type and allocation faces, expand the discrete risk by a vector Stein identity within each stratum, use the certified \(c^\dagger\) LP sequence to select the normalizer, and pass the primal and dual games to a stratified diffusion-control or spectral value problem with face and corner compatibility conditions.

definitions.name: Contrast-score feedback and converse handle
definitions.construction: Begin with the vector of centered arm scores generated by \(q^\star\); derive an orbit-saddle posterior mean or feedback correction from the limiting value function, lift that correction to finite \(n\), and discretize the squared ground state or dual occupation measure into a least-favorable prior on response-type counts.

definitions.name: Rational-contrast exact grid-action LP
definitions.construction:
Fix \(K\geq2\), \(n,M\geq1\), and a rational nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\in\mathbb Q^K\).  Put \(h_c=L_c/2\) and
\[
 \Gamma_{M,c}=\{-h_c+jh_c/M:j=0,\ldots,2M\}.
\]
Minimize \(u\) over \(\pi_r\geq0\) and \(w_{r,x,g}\geq0\), subject to
\[
 \sum_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}}\pi_r=1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{g\in\Gamma_{M,c}}w_{r,x,g}=\pi_r
 \quad\text{for every }(r,x),
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}}\sum_x\sum_{g\in\Gamma_{M,c}}
 P_m(x\mid r)w_{r,x,g}\{g-\tau_c(m)\}^2\leq u
 \quad\text{for every }m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}.
\]
The value of this finite grid-action linear program is \(\Lambda_{n,M}(c)\).

statements.statement: For every fixed \(n\), \(K\ge2\), and contrast \(c\), begin with nature choosing a complete labeled schedule \(z\in\mathcal T_K^n\), an arbitrary assignment law \(\mathcal D\), and an arbitrary estimator \(\widehat\tau\). Averaging a procedure over common permutations of unit labels is lossless, and the symmetrized risk is constant on each unit-permutation orbit of schedules. Consequently, with \(m_t=\#\{i:t_i=t\}\), \(\tau_c(z)=\tau_c(m)\), and the labeled minimax risk equals the explicit orbit game: \(\rho_n(c)=G_n(c)\). A symmetrized design is exactly a mixture \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal R_{n,K})\) of uniform assignments conditional on \(r\), and a nonrandomized invariant estimator is \(\delta(r,x)\). The compact convex game admits a minimax procedure and a least-favorable prior on \(\mathcal M_{n,K}\) forming a saddle point.
statements.justification: This theorem converts an unrestricted and exponentially presented experimental decision problem into an explicit finite object that supports computation, asymptotics, and a matched converse.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 1--3, proof of Theorem 2, and Sections 5--6) obtain their scalar two-arm reduction from a least-favorable prior and transformed variables \(S_i\) that are ancillary for the design under that prior. Hull (2026, Theorem 1, proof Steps 1--3) instead averages independent per-unit swaps of the two potential-outcome coordinates together with assignment-bit exclusive-or, and then averages over unit labels. Neither route supplies the fixed-contrast \(2^K\)-type orbit likelihood or a lossless multi-arm saddle point.
statements.consumer: The exact game supplies the finite benchmark needed to audit joint design and analysis choices for a four-arm binary endpoint such as ACTG 175.
statements.proof_tex:
Let \(\mathfrak S_n\) act simultaneously on schedules, assignments, and observed outcome vectors by
\[
 (\gamma z)_i=t_{\gamma^{-1}(i)},\qquad
 (\gamma A)_i=A_{\gamma^{-1}(i)},\qquad
 (\gamma y)_i=y_{\gamma^{-1}(i)}.
\]
The causal contrast is invariant under this action, since
\[
 \tau_c(\gamma z)
 =\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_{\gamma^{-1}(i),a}
 =\tau_c(z).
\]

Fix a labeled procedure \(p=(\mathcal D,f)\).  Draw \(\Gamma\) uniformly from \(\mathfrak S_n\), draw \(B\sim\mathcal D\), assign \(A=\Gamma B\), and, after observing \(y\), use the randomized action
\[
 U=f(\Gamma^{-1}A,\Gamma^{-1}y).
\]
Under schedule \(z\), inverse-permuting the observed data produces exactly the data generated by \(p\) under \(\Gamma^{-1}z\).  Therefore
\[
 \mathbb E_z\!\left[\{U-\tau_c(z)\}^2\right]
 =\frac1{n!}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathfrak S_n}
 R_n(\mathcal D,f;\gamma^{-1}z).
\]
The marginal law of the symmetrized assignment is
\[
 \overline{\mathcal D}(A)
 =\frac1{n!}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathfrak S_n}\mathcal D(\gamma^{-1}A).
\]
When \(\overline{\mathcal D}(A)>0\), define
\[
 \bar f(A,y)=
 \frac{\sum_{\gamma\in\mathfrak S_n}\mathcal D(\gamma^{-1}A)
 f(\gamma^{-1}A,\gamma^{-1}y)}
 {\sum_{\gamma\in\mathfrak S_n}\mathcal D(\gamma^{-1}A)},
\]
and define \(\bar f\) arbitrarily in \([-L_c/2,L_c/2]\) when the denominator is zero.  The conditional weights in this average depend only on \(A\), and hence do not depend on the unknown schedule.  Conditional Jensen's inequality gives, for every \(z\),
\[
 R_n(\overline{\mathcal D},\bar f;z)
 \le \frac1{n!}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathfrak S_n}
 R_n(\mathcal D,f;\gamma^{-1}z)
 \le \max_{z'}R_n(\mathcal D,f;z').
\]
A change of summation variable shows
\(\overline{\mathcal D}(\eta A)=\overline{\mathcal D}(A)\) and
\(\bar f(\eta A,\eta y)=\bar f(A,y)\) for every \(\eta\in\mathfrak S_n\).  Thus symmetrization is lossless for worst-case risk, produces a deterministic invariant estimator, and makes risk constant on unit-permutation orbits of schedules.

The schedule orbits are exactly the response-type count vectors \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}\).  On the orbit indexed by \(m\),
\[
 \tau_c(z)=\frac1n\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_K}m_t
 \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_a=\tau_c(m).
\]
The assignment orbits are exactly the allocation vectors \(r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}\).  An orbit with allocation \(r\) contains \(n!/\prod_a r_a!\) assignments.  Hence every invariant assignment law has the unique representation: first draw \(r\) with probabilities \(\pi_r\), then draw uniformly conditional on \(r\).  Conversely, every \(\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal R_{n,K})\) defines an invariant design.  The observed-data orbits are exactly \((r,x)\), because the counts of pairs \((A_i,Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}})=(a,1)\) and \((a,0)\) are \(x_a\) and \(r_a-x_a\).  Thus every deterministic invariant estimator is, and every map \(\delta(r,x)\) defines, an invariant estimator.

Fix \(m,r,x\).  For any \(h\in\mathcal H(m,r,x)\), the number of assignments that send the \(m_t\) labeled units of type \(t\) to arms with cell counts \(h_{t,a}\) is
\[
 \prod_{t\in\mathcal T_K}\frac{m_t!}{\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}h_{t,a}!}.
\]
Summing this count over the fiber \(\mathcal H(m,r,x)\) and dividing by the orbit size \(n!/\prod_a r_a!\) gives
\[
 P_m(x\mid r)=\frac{\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}r_a!}{n!}
 \sum_{h\in\mathcal H(m,r,x)}
 \prod_{t\in\mathcal T_K}\frac{m_t!}{\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_K}h_{t,a}!},
\]
which is the frozen orbit likelihood.  Consequently, the risk of \((\pi,\delta)\) is exactly
\[
 \sum_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,K}}\pi_r
 \sum_xP_m(x\mid r)\{\delta(r,x)-\tau_c(m)\}^2.
\]
Every orbit procedure is a labeled procedure, while the preceding symmetrization shows that every labeled procedure is weakly dominated in worst-case risk by an orbit procedure.  The two inequalities imply
\[
 \rho_n(c)=G_n(c).
\]

It remains to prove attainment and the saddle assertion.  The set \(\mathscr P\) of pairs \((\pi,\delta)\) is a finite product of compact simplexes and compact intervals.  If \(v_m(p)\) denotes the risk at \(m\), continuity and finiteness of \(\mathcal M_{n,K}\) imply that
\[
 V=\min_{p\in\mathscr P}\max_{m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}}v_m(p)
\]
is attained at some \(p^\star\).  Although the raw coordinates \((\pi,\delta)\) do not make the payoff jointly convex, the attainable upper risk set is convex.  Indeed, for \(p_j=(\pi_j,\delta_j)\), \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), set
\[
 \pi_r=\lambda\pi_{0r}+(1-\lambda)\pi_{1r},
 \qquad
 \delta(r,x)=
 \frac{\lambda\pi_{0r}\delta_0(r,x)+(1-\lambda)\pi_{1r}\delta_1(r,x)}{\pi_r}
\]
when \(\pi_r>0\), with arbitrary \(\delta(r,x)\) when \(\pi_r=0\).  Convexity of squared loss gives simultaneously for every \(m\)
\[
 v_m(p)\le\lambda v_m(p_0)+(1-\lambda)v_m(p_1).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \mathcal U=\left\{u\in[0,L_c^2]^{\mathcal M_{n,K}}:
 \text{some }p\in\mathscr P\text{ satisfies }v_m(p)\le u_m
 \text{ for all }m\right\}
\]
is nonempty, compact, convex, and coordinatewise upper comprehensive.

We now derive a least-favorable prior by separation.  Let \(d=|\mathcal M_{n,K}|\), let \(\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^d\), and, for \(\varepsilon>0\), put \(y_\varepsilon=(V-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1\).  By the definition of \(V\), \(y_\varepsilon\notin\mathcal U\).  Let \(u_\varepsilon\) be its Euclidean projection onto \(\mathcal U\) and set \(\eta_\varepsilon=u_\varepsilon-y_\varepsilon\).  Upper comprehensiveness implies \(\eta_\varepsilon\ge0\) coordinatewise: otherwise increasing a deficient coordinate to the corresponding coordinate of \(y_\varepsilon\) would stay in \(\mathcal U\) and shorten the distance.  The projection inequality gives
\[
 \eta_\varepsilon\mathbin{\cdot}(u-u_\varepsilon)\ge0
 \qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.
\]
Since \(y_\varepsilon\notin\mathcal U\), \(\eta_\varepsilon\ne0\).  Normalize
\(\mu_\varepsilon=\eta_\varepsilon/\sum_m\eta_{\varepsilon,m}\).  Along a convergent subsequence as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), \(\mu_\varepsilon\to\mu^\star\in\Delta(\mathcal M_{n,K})\), and the preceding inequality yields
\[
 \sum_m\mu_m^\star u_m\ge V
 \qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.
\]
Applying this to every risk vector and to \(p^\star\), whose risk coordinates are at most \(V\), gives
\[
 \sum_m\mu_m^\star v_m(p)\ge V
 =\sum_m\mu_m^\star v_m(p^\star),
 \qquad v_m(p^\star)\le V.
\]
Consequently, for every prior \(\mu\) and procedure \(p\),
\[
 \sum_m\mu_m v_m(p^\star)
 \le\sum_m\mu_m^\star v_m(p^\star)
 \le\sum_m\mu_m^\star v_m(p).
\]
Thus \((p^\star,\mu^\star)\) is a saddle point and \(\mu^\star\) is least favorable.  No exposure-positivity, rank, or inverse condition is needed: zero allocation counts are permitted, \(0!=1\), and values of an estimator on zero-probability observations are immaterial.  As a boundary check, when \(n=1\) and \(r\) assigns the sole unit to arm \(a\), the contingency-table formula reduces to the point mass \(x_a=t_a\); the all-zero and all-one response types remain in the state space.

statements.statement: The exact response-type game is a strict domain extension of the published two-arm scalar minimax theorem. As an explicitly non-novel sanity and regression clause, when \(K=2\) and \(c=(1,-1)\), this proposal's orbit experiment retains the four distinct counts \(m_{(0,0)},m_{(0,1)},m_{(1,0)},m_{(1,1)}\) in the likelihood \(P_m(x\mid r)\). In particular, no aggregation by individual-effect class is asserted to identify that likelihood kernel. Instead, composing the exact equality \(\rho_n(c)=G_n(c)\) with Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen's published two-arm minimax theorem (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and Section 6) recovers at the minimax-value level their scalar value based on \(X_2=p_++\operatorname{Binomial}(r_0,1/2)\) for estimating \((p_+-p_-)/n\), where \(p_++p_-+r_0=n\). Consequently, \(C_0(c)=1\) and \(d_n(c)=C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), with \(C_A\) determined by the published scalar Airy ground-state problem. For every fixed \(K\ge3\) and every nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\), the same theorem additionally proves equality of the unrestricted labeled-schedule risk and the explicit joint \(2^K\)-response-type orbit game, including arbitrary assignment dependence and possibly biased estimators; those \(K\ge3\) cases are outside the published two-arm theorem. This statement does not assert that the multi-arm game is scalar-nonrepresentable.
statements.justification: The strict-extension result fixes the published binary minimax value as a regression target without collapsing the four-count orbit likelihood, and isolates the new labeled-schedule and orbit-game equality for every fixed multi-arm contrast.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and Section 6) prove the scalar binary minimax value only for two arms; the strict extension is the exact unrestricted equality for \(K\ge3\), not the already published scalar value or Airy expansion.
statements.consumer: It lets the three-arm rational diagnostic and the four-arm ACTG 175 analysis inherit a verified unrestricted decision problem while preserving the published binary game as a regression case.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
First take \(K=2\) and \(c=(1,-1)\).  Directly from the orbit target,
\[
 \tau_c(m)
 =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t\in\{0,1\}^2}m_t(t_1-t_2)
 =\frac{m_{(1,0)}-m_{(0,1)}}{n}
 =\frac{p_+-p_-}{n},
\]
and \(r_0=m_{(0,0)}+m_{(1,1)}\), so \(p_++p_-+r_0=n\).  This aggregation is valid for the target only.  Indeed, in the orbit likelihood
\[
 P_m(x\mid r)
 =\frac{\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_2}r_a!}{n!}
 \sum_{h\in\mathcal H(m,r,x)}
 \prod_{t\in\mathcal T_2}\frac{m_t!}{\prod_{a\in\mathcal A_2}h_{t,a}!},
\]
the factorials \(m_t!\) and the row constraints
\(\sum_a h_{t,a}=m_t\) are still indexed separately by
\(t=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\).  Hence neither the likelihood definition nor the exact-game theorem asserts that \(P_m(x\mid r)\) is determined by \((p_+,p_-,r_0)\).

The exact response-type game theorem gives
\[
 \rho_n((1,-1))=G_n((1,-1)).
\]
The embedded two-arm converse theorem applies with \(|S_c|=2\).  Its equality clause identifies this value with \(C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}\); here
\[
 L_c=|1|+|-1|=2,
 \qquad
 C_0(c)=\frac{L_c^2}{4}=1,
\]
so the value is exactly the unrestricted binary risk \(\rho_{n,2}\).  The published two-arm result incorporated in that established theorem identifies this minimax value with the scalar experiment
\[
 X_2=p_++\operatorname{Binomial}(r_0,1/2)
\]
for estimating \((p_+-p_-)/n\), and yields
\[
 \rho_n((1,-1))
 =\frac{1}{n}-C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
Therefore, from the definition \(d_n(c)=C_0(c)/n-\rho_n(c)\),
\[
 d_n((1,-1))=C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
This is a composition at the level of minimax values; it does not collapse the four-count orbit likelihood.

Now fix \(K\geq3\) and a nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\).  The exact response-type game theorem applies without any restriction on dependence among assignments and without an unbiasedness restriction on the estimator.  It gives
\[
 \rho_n(c)=G_n(c),
\]
where nature ranges over \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,K}\), the count simplex generated by all \(|\mathcal T_K|=2^K\) binary response types, and where \(G_n(c)\) is the explicit orbit game using \(P_m(x\mid r)\).  The cited published theorem concerns only the two-arm scalar experiment, whereas this equality covers every fixed \(K\geq3\) and every such contrast.  Thus the exact response-type theorem is a strict extension in treatment-domain scope.  This conclusion neither rules out some other scalar representation of a multi-arm value nor asserts that one exists.

No positivity, overlap, rank, or inverse condition is used: the design class is unrestricted, allocation cells with \(r_a=0\) are permitted by the exact orbit game, and the all-zero and all-one response types remain in \(\mathcal T_K\).  This also supplies the relevant boundary check. \(\square\)

statements.statement: If \(\mathfrak G_c\) acts transitively on \(S_c\), then \(|c_a|\) is constant over \(a\in S_c\), and the numbers of positive and negative active coefficients are equal. For \(K=3\) and \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), \(\mathfrak G_{c^\dagger}\) has exactly the two arm orbits \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\). Therefore a quotient based solely on signed contrast-preserving arm relabelings cannot merge arm \(1\) with arms \(2\) and \(3\) in the \(c^\dagger\) orbit game. This is an independent orbit diagnostic and not a claim about Hull's coordinatewise swap construction or about scalar representations in general.
statements.justification: The proposition determines exactly which ordinary arm-label symmetries may be used to compress the three-arm diagnostic without changing its contrast.
statements.gap: Bai (2023, Theorem 2.1 and Remark 2.2) shows how invariance can reduce a decision problem, but does not calculate the signed contrast stabilizer or its orbits for the fixed multi-arm response-type game.
statements.consumer: It tells the exact-orbit computation that arms \(2\) and \(3\) may be pooled by symmetry while arm \(1\) must retain a separate allocation label.
statements.proof_tex:
\paragraph{Proof.}
By Definition~\(\mathrm{def{:}signed\text{-}contrast\text{-}stabilizer}\), for every \(\sigma\in\mathfrak G_c\) there is a sign \(s_\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) such that
\[
c_{\sigma(a)}=s_\sigma c_a
\qquad\text{for every }a\in\mathcal A_K.
\]
Consequently, if \(a\in S_c\), then
\[
|c_{\sigma(a)}|=|s_\sigma c_a|=|c_a|>0,
\]
so \(\sigma(a)\in S_c\). Thus the action preserves the active support.

Suppose now that this action is transitive on \(S_c\). For any \(a,b\in S_c\), transitivity supplies \(\sigma\in\mathfrak G_c\) with \(\sigma(a)=b\). The preceding identity gives
\[
|c_b|=|c_{\sigma(a)}|=|c_a|.
\]
Hence there is a number \(d>0\) such that \(|c_a|=d\) for every \(a\in S_c\). Define
\[
N_+=\#\{a\in S_c:c_a>0\},
\qquad
N_-=\#\{a\in S_c:c_a<0\}.
\]
Because \(c\) is a contrast, \(\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_a=0\), while coefficients outside \(S_c\) vanish. Therefore
\[
0=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_a
 =\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a
 =dN_+-dN_-
 =d(N_+-N_-).
\]
Division by \(d>0\) yields \(N_+=N_-\).

For the diagnostic contrast \(c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), let \(\sigma\in\mathfrak G_{c^\dagger}\) and let \(s\) be its associated sign. If \(s=-1\), then the defining relation at \(a=1\) would require
\[
c^\dagger_{\sigma(1)}=-c^\dagger_1=-1,
\]
but none of the three coordinates of \(c^\dagger\) equals \(-1\). Hence \(s=1\). The value \(1\) occurs at the unique arm \(1\), so
\[
c^\dagger_{\sigma(1)}=c^\dagger_1=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sigma(1)=1.
\]
The permutation \(\sigma\) may therefore only fix or exchange arms \(2\) and \(3\). Conversely, both the identity and the transposition \((2\ 3)\) preserve \(c^\dagger\). It follows that
\[
\mathfrak G_{c^\dagger}=\{\operatorname{id},(2\ 3)\},
\]
whose arm orbits are exactly \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\). A quotient whose equivalence relation is generated solely by this group can identify only elements in the same group orbit, and hence cannot merge arm \(1\) with arm \(2\) or arm \(3\).

\paragraph{Scope and sanity checks.}
This argument uses only that \(K\) is finite and fixed and that \(c\) is a nonzero, zero-sum contrast; there are no probabilistic support, positivity, overlap, rank, asymptotic, or boundary assumptions. For \(c^\dagger\), the unequal active magnitudes and the unequal sign counts also independently rule out transitivity by the first part. The conclusion concerns only quotients generated by signed contrast-preserving arm relabelings, so it makes no assertion about coordinatewise swap constructions or other possible scalar representations.

statements.statement: Under fixed \(K\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}n\rho_n(c)=C_0(c)=\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|c_a|\right)^2.\] Independent assignment supported on \(S_c\) with \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) and the projected rule \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star\) satisfies \(\max_{z\in\mathcal T_K^n}R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star;z)\le C_0(c)/n\). Because every target \(\tau_c(z)\) lies in \([-L_c/2,L_c/2]\), projection onto this interval cannot increase pointwise squared loss, so \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star\) belongs to the same minimax estimator action space. Conversely, every sequence of randomized designs and possibly biased estimators has asymptotic worst-case labeled-schedule risk at least \(C_0(c)/n+o(n^{-1})\).
statements.justification: It certifies the best robustness constant and the allocation rule before the genuinely nonclassical finite-sample correction is studied.
statements.gap: Bai (2023) derives Neyman allocation for linear procedures under a different superpopulation adversary, while the two 2026 papers prove unrestricted minimaxity only for two arms.
statements.consumer: For ACTG 175, it gives the worst-case allocation benchmark for a prespecified regimen-versus-average contrast rather than default equal allocation.
statements.proof_tex:
Let
\[
 \widetilde\tau=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i,
 \qquad
 Z_i=\sum_{a\in S_c}
 \frac{c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}}{q_a^\star}
 \bigl(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1/2\bigr).
\]
Because \(c\neq0\), one has \(L_c>0\).  For every \(a\in S_c\), the definition \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c\) therefore gives \(q_a^\star>0\), so all displayed divisions are valid.  Under the independent design in \(\mathrm{def:first\text{-}order\text{-}procedure}\), and for a fixed response schedule \(z\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{\mathcal D}(Z_i\mid z)
 &=\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a(t_{i,a}-1/2)\\
 &=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}c_at_{i,a}=:\mu_i.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses \(c_a=0\) off \(S_c\) and \(\sum_a c_a=0\).  Hence
\[
 \mathbb E_{\mathcal D}(\widetilde\tau\mid z)
 =\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i=\tau_c(z).
\]
Since \(t_{i,a}\in\{0,1\}\), the identity \((t_{i,a}-1/2)^2=1/4\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{\mathcal D}(Z_i^2\mid z)
 &=\frac14\sum_{a\in S_c}\frac{c_a^2}{q_a^\star}
 =\frac14\sum_{a\in S_c}L_c|c_a|\\
 &=\frac{L_c^2}{4}=C_0(c).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Assignments are independent across units, so the variables \(Z_i\) are independent conditional on the fixed schedule.  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R_n(\mathcal D,\widetilde\tau;z)
 &=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n
 \operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(Z_i\mid z)\\
 &=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\{C_0(c)-\mu_i^2\}
 \leq\frac{C_0(c)}n.
 \end{aligned}
\]

Write \(P_c=\{a:c_a>0\}\) and \(N_c=\{a:c_a<0\}\).  The zero-sum identity implies
\[
 \sum_{a\in P_c}c_a
 =-\sum_{a\in N_c}c_a=\frac{L_c}{2}.
\]
For every binary response vector \(t_i\), it follows that
\[
 -\frac{L_c}{2}\leq\sum_a c_at_{i,a}\leq\frac{L_c}{2},
\]
and averaging over units yields \(\tau_c(z)\in[-L_c/2,L_c/2]\).  Metric projection onto a closed interval cannot increase squared distance from any point of that interval.  Thus the projected estimator \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star\) belongs to the stipulated estimator action space and satisfies
\[
 \max_{z\in\mathcal T_K^n}
 R_n(\mathcal D,\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{cHT}}^\star;z)
 \leq\frac{C_0(c)}n.
\]
In particular, \(\rho_n(c)\leq C_0(c)/n\).

We next retain a direct first-order converse based only on a prior over fixed binary schedules.  Since \(K\) is fixed, \(s:=|S_c|\) is fixed.  Put \(\epsilon_n=n^{-1/4}/4\) and
\[
 w(u)=\frac{15}{16}(1-u^2)^2\mathbf 1\{|u|\leq1\},
 \qquad
 J=\int_{-1}^1\frac{\{w'(u)\}^2}{w(u)}\,du<\infty.
\]
For each \(a\in S_c\), independently draw \(P_a\) with density
\[
 p\longmapsto\epsilon_n^{-1}w\!\left(\frac{p-1/2}{\epsilon_n}\right),
\]
and set \(P_a=1/2\) for \(a\notin S_c\).  Independently draw \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) identically and uniformly on \([0,1]\), and define
\[
 Y_i(a)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\leq P_a\}.
\]
After \((P,U)\) is drawn, this construction is a fixed element of \(\mathcal T_K^n\); thus it is a legitimate prior on the finite schedule space and is independent of every admissible assignment law.

Define
\[
 \vartheta(P)=\sum_{a\in S_c}c_aP_a,
 \qquad
 g_P(u)=\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\mathbf 1\{u\leq P_a\}.
\]
Conditional on \(P\),
\[
 \tau_c(z)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ng_P(U_i),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\{\tau_c(z)\mid P\}=\vartheta(P).
\]
The zero-sum identity makes \(g_P\) vanish outside
\([\min_{a\in S_c}P_a,\max_{a\in S_c}P_a]\), an interval of length at most \(2\epsilon_n\).  Also \(|g_P(u)|\leq L_c/2\).  Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 e_n^2
 &:=\mathbb E\{\tau_c(z)-\vartheta(P)\}^2\\
 &=\frac1n\mathbb E\{\operatorname{Var}(g_P(U_1)\mid P)\}
 \leq\frac{L_c^2\epsilon_n}{2n},
 \end{aligned}
\]
so \(e_n=O(n^{-5/8})=o(n^{-1/2})\).

Fix an arbitrary assignment law \(\mathcal D\), allowing arbitrary dependence among the assignments, and put \(s_a=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}r_a\).  Conditional on \((P,A)\), the observed outcomes are independent and satisfy
\[
 Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(P_{A_i}).
\]
By the symmetry and compact support of \(w\),
\[
 \kappa_n
 :=\mathbb E\!\left\{\frac1{P_a(1-P_a)}\right\}
 =4+O(\epsilon_n^2).
\]
For \(a\in S_c\), let \(S_a\) be the score of the joint prior--likelihood density with respect to \(P_a\).  Conditional mean-zero of each Bernoulli likelihood score, independence of the arm priors, and independence of the observed outcomes conditional on \((P,A)\) show that the score covariance matrix is diagonal, with
\[
 I_a:=\mathbb E(S_a^2)
 =\kappa_ns_a+\frac{J}{\epsilon_n^2}>0.
\]
Thus no exposure-positivity condition is required for this converse; the prior-information term makes every denominator positive even when \(s_a=0\).

Let \(T=T(A,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\) be any possibly biased estimator.  The functions \(w\) and \(w'\) vanish at both endpoints of their support.  Integration by parts in \(P_a\), with no boundary term, gives
\[
 \mathbb E(TS_a)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\{\vartheta(P)S_a\}=-c_a,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[\{T-\vartheta(P)\}S_a]=c_a.
\]
For every vector \(v=(v_a)_{a\in S_c}\), Cauchy--Schwarz and diagonality of the score covariance give
\[
 \mathbb E\{T-\vartheta(P)\}^2
 \geq\frac{(v^\top c)^2}{\sum_{a\in S_c}v_a^2I_a}.
\]
Taking \(v_a=c_a/I_a\), and then applying Cauchy--Schwarz to the vectors \((|c_a|/\sqrt{I_a})_a\) and \((\sqrt{I_a})_a\), yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\{T-\vartheta(P)\}^2
 &\geq\sum_{a\in S_c}\frac{c_a^2}{I_a}
 \geq\frac{L_c^2}{\sum_{a\in S_c}I_a}\\
 &\geq\frac{L_c^2}{\kappa_n n+sJ/\epsilon_n^2}
 =\frac{C_0(c)}n+o(n^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\sum_{a\in S_c}s_a\leq n\), \(\kappa_n=4+O(n^{-1/2})\), and \(sJ/\epsilon_n^2=O(n^{1/2})\).

The reverse triangle inequality in \(L^2\) now gives, uniformly over \(\mathcal D\) and \(T\),
\[
 \left[\mathbb E\{T-\tau_c(z)\}^2\right]^{1/2}
 \geq
 \frac{L_c}{\sqrt{\kappa_n n+sJ/\epsilon_n^2}}-e_n.
\]
The first term is asymptotic to \(L_c/(2\sqrt n)\), while \(e_n=o(n^{-1/2})\).  Squaring the positive part therefore proves
\[
 \mathbb E\{T-\tau_c(z)\}^2
 \geq\frac{C_0(c)}n+o(n^{-1}).
\]
The maximum over fixed schedules dominates the average under the constructed prior.  Taking the infimum over all assignment laws and all possibly biased estimators proves the stated unrestricted first-order lower bound.

There is also a sharper finite-sample converse.  By \(\mathrm{thm:embedded\text{-}two\text{-}arm\text{-}converse}\), for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
 \rho_n(c)\geq C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}.
\]
Its published two-arm consequence is
\[
 \rho_n(c)
 \geq\frac{C_0(c)}n-C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}),
\]
which in particular recovers the preceding \(C_0(c)/n+o(n^{-1})\) converse.  When \(|S_c|=2\), the embedded theorem states equality.  When \(|S_c|\geq3\), only the displayed inequality is used: no second-order equality is claimed.

Combining either first-order converse with the finite-sample upper certificate yields
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}n\rho_n(c)
 =C_0(c)=\frac{L_c^2}{4}
 =\frac14\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|c_a|\right)^2.
\]
The equality \(\rho_n(c)=G_n(c)\) from \(\mathrm{thm:exact\text{-}response\text{-}type\text{-}game}\) transfers the same first-order value and the finite-sample certificates to the explicit orbit game.

Finally, the allocation choice has a matching convex optimality certificate.  For any allocation vector \(q\) with \(q_a>0\) on \(S_c\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \frac14\sum_{a\in S_c}\frac{c_a^2}{q_a}
 \geq\frac14
 \frac{\left(\sum_{a\in S_c}|c_a|\right)^2}
 {\sum_{a\in S_c}q_a}
 \geq\frac{L_c^2}{4}.
\]
Equality holds precisely when no probability is assigned outside \(S_c\) and \(q_a\) is proportional to \(|c_a|\) on \(S_c\), namely \(q=q^\star\).  This completes the first-order saddle and allocation-optimality proof.

statements.statement: For \(K=3\), \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), and every \(n,M\ge1\), the grid-action program defining \(\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\) is a finite linear program with rational coefficients and \[\rho_n^\dagger\le\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\le\rho_n^\dagger+\frac{2}{M}+\frac{1}{M^2}.\] Consequently, choosing \(M=n^2\) yields exact-rational primal and dual certificates whose discretization error is \(o(n^{-4/3})\), so the sequence \(n^{4/3}\{n^{-1}-\Lambda_{n,n^2}^\dagger\}\) is a valid early diagnostic for, but not an assumption of, the \(4/3\) exponent. The LP retains the all-zero and all-one response types and every response-type count vector in \(\mathcal M_{n,3}\).
statements.justification: The proposition turns small-\(n\) numerics into certified falsification evidence with an error smaller than the published two-arm second-order scale.
statements.gap: Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Appendix A and Section 3) study a scalar finite program and its numerical scaling, while Hull (2026, Theorem 1) resolves a two-arm endpoint game analytically; no cited work gives a rational multi-arm orbit LP hierarchy or an error bracket to the unrestricted continuous-action game.
statements.consumer: The diagnostic prevents a long simplex-PDE analysis from proceeding under an incorrect exponent or a falsely multidimensional value.
statements.proof_tex:
For \(c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), \(L_{c^\dagger}=2\), so both \(\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\) and every admissible continuous estimate lie in \([-1,1]\).  Every indexing set in the program is finite.  The factorial formula makes \(P_m(x\mid r)\) rational, while \(\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\) and every \(g\in\Gamma_M\) are rational.  Thus every objective and constraint coefficient is rational.  The action \(g=0\) is in \(\Gamma_M\) and gives a feasible rule with \(u\le1\); for minimization one may therefore restrict \(u\) to \([0,1]\).  All other variables lie in finite products of simplexes, so the relevant feasible set is a compact rational polytope.

For completeness, rational primal and dual certificates follow by an elementary elimination argument.  Put the finite program in equality-and-inequality form and eliminate its variables one at a time by Fourier--Motzkin elimination, retaining the objective-coordinate variable.  At each step the new inequalities are nonnegative rational linear combinations of preceding inequalities.  The final feasible objective set is a one-dimensional rational polyhedron, whose finite attained lower endpoint is rational.  Back-substitution at rational endpoints produces a rational primal optimizer.  Recording the nonnegative rational combinations that produce the endpoint inequality gives feasible rational dual multipliers with that same objective value; weak duality then certifies optimality of both.  Hence the program admits exact-rational primal and dual certificates.

We next compare it with the continuous orbit game.  Let \((\pi,w,u)\) be feasible.  If \(\pi_r>0\), define
\[
 \kappa_{r,x}(g)=\frac{w_{r,x,g}}{\pi_r},
 \qquad
 \bar\delta(r,x)=\sum_{g\in\Gamma_M}\kappa_{r,x}(g)g;
\]
when \(\pi_r=0\), choose \(\kappa_{r,x}\) arbitrarily.  The constraints
\(\sum_gw_{r,x,g}=\pi_r\) make \(\kappa_{r,x}\) a probability kernel selected after observing \((r,x)\).  For every \(m,r,x\), the conditional variance identity gives
\[
 \sum_g\kappa_{r,x}(g)\{g-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2
 =\{\bar\delta(r,x)-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2
 +\sum_g\kappa_{r,x}(g)\{g-\bar\delta(r,x)\}^2.
\]
Because \(\bar\delta(r,x)\in[-1,1]\), it is an admissible deterministic continuous action.  Dropping the nonnegative variance term and using the exact-game equality gives
\[
 \rho_n^\dagger=G_n(c^\dagger)\le u.
\]
Taking the infimum over feasible grid programs proves
\(\rho_n^\dagger\le\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger\).

Conversely, let \((\pi,\delta)\) be a minimax continuous orbit procedure, whose existence was proved in the exact response-type game theorem.  Let \(Q_M(v)\) be a nearest point of \(\Gamma_M\) to \(v\in[-1,1]\), with any fixed tie rule.  The mesh is \(1/M\), so
\[
 e(r,x)=Q_M(\delta(r,x))-\delta(r,x),
 \qquad |e(r,x)|\le\frac1{2M}.
\]
Set
\(w_{r,x,g}=\pi_r\mathbf 1\{g=Q_M(\delta(r,x))\}\).  This satisfies every normalization constraint.  For every \(m,r,x\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \{Q_M(\delta)-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2
 -\{\delta-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2
 &=2e\{\delta-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}+e^2\\
 &\le2|e|\,|\delta-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)|+e^2\\
 &\le\frac2M+\frac1{4M^2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
because \(|\delta-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)|\le2\).  Averaging against \(\pi_rP_m(x\mid r)\), using \(\sum_r\pi_r=1\) and \(\sum_xP_m(x\mid r)=1\), and maximizing over \(m\) gives
\[
 \Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger
 \le\rho_n^\dagger+\frac2M+\frac1{4M^2}
 \le\rho_n^\dagger+\frac2M+\frac1{M^2}.
\]
For \(M=n^2\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &n^{4/3}\left|\{n^{-1}-\Lambda_{n,n^2}^\dagger\}
 -\{n^{-1}-\rho_n^\dagger\}\right|\\
 &\qquad=n^{4/3}\{\Lambda_{n,n^2}^\dagger-\rho_n^\dagger\}
 \le2n^{-2/3}+n^{-8/3}\longrightarrow0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus the certified sequence has the same \(n^{4/3}\)-scale behavior as the unrestricted improvement without presupposing that \(4/3\) is the correct exponent.  Finally, the LP constraints are indexed by every \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,3}\), and the likelihood uses every \(t\in\mathcal T_3\).  In particular, schedules concentrated on the all-zero or all-one response type remain present.

statements.statement:
For every fixed nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\) with \(|S_c|\geq3\), the universal second-order rate theorem proves
\[
 0<\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{4/3}d_n(c)
 \leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{4/3}d_n(c)
 \leq C_0(c)C_A,
\]
and hence \(d_n(c)=\Theta(n^{-4/3})\); every regularly varying normalizer that yields a finite positive limit has index \(4/3\). Writing \(x_n(c)=n^{4/3}d_n(c)\), its subsequential-limit set is a nonempty compact subset of the positive compact interval supplied by this bracket. A regularly varying normalization with a finite positive limit exists if and only if \(x_n(c)\) is slowly varying; thus, in the nonconvergent branch, a genuinely nonconvergent slowly varying correction exists exactly when \(x_n(c)\) itself is slowly varying.

For every rational nonzero zero-sum contrast, take grid resolution \(M=n\) in the exact-rational certificate theorem. The normalized grid-value improvement, the normalized upper-procedure improvement, the normalized prior-lower-bound improvement, and \(x_n(c)\) have pairwise distance \(o(1)\). Consequently they have exactly the same subsequential-limit set and converge simultaneously, with the same limit whenever convergence occurs. For every real nonzero zero-sum contrast, choose rational zero-sum contrasts \(c^{(n)}\) with
\[
 \eta_n=\frac{L_{c-c^{(n)}}}{2}=o(n^{-5/6})
\]
and again take grid resolution \(M=n\). The rational-approximation risk bracket and the corresponding improvement bracket have width \(o(n^{-4/3})\); after multiplication by \(n^{4/3}\), both endpoints and \(x_n(c)\) therefore have the same subsequential-limit set and convergence behavior. These claims retain all response-type count vectors and impose no positivity or support restriction on the unrestricted minimax design beyond the fixed nonzero contrast.

The residual questions are whether \(x_n(c)\) converges, what its sharp limit or exact subsequential-limit set is, whether a nonconvergent \(x_n(c)\) is slowly varying, and what limiting value problem, if any, governs these quantities. Any such value problem must be derived with existence, admissibility, and uniqueness, and must decide whether active simplex faces and corners yield a multidimensional free-boundary Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman problem, an elliptic cone spectral problem, a separable collection of scalar layers, or no stable limit of these forms. The exact \(K=3\), \(c=c^\dagger\) calculations through \(n\leq5\) remain a finite-sample showcase of the general rational certificates only; they are not used to infer a cross-\(n\) limit. The certificates and the scalar-score nonpreservation witness establish neither convergence, optimizer or prior convergence, a sharp constant, an analytic feedback rule, nor a limiting operator.
statements.justification: The universal theorem fixes the positive \(n^{-4/3}\) order, and the finite-program certificates now reproduce the normalized risk up to \(o(1)\) for every rational contrast and, through continuity brackets, every real contrast. The remaining contribution is genuinely cross-population: convergence, the sharp constant or exact subsequential set, and the face--corner mechanism.
statements.gap: Each exact program certifies one population size. Neither its vanishing within-size primal--dual gap nor the rational-approximation transfer compares adjacent values of \(n\), proves tightness of optimizers or priors, or derives a compatible limiting generator on simplex faces and corners. The scalar-score witness rules out only one reduction and supplies no positive operator theory.
statements.consumer: For ACTG 175-type multi-arm contrasts, the existing results already give an explicit \(n^{-4/3}\)-order improvement and computable matched risk brackets; solving this residual question would determine the sharp second-order correction and whether an analytic feedback design can replace the finite programs.

statements.statement:
A rigorous partial answer is available.  Fix \(K\geq2\) and a nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\).

First, if \(|S_c|=2\), then contrast-weighted independent assignment, with probability \(1/2\) on each active arm, and the coefficient-rescaled published two-arm posterior-mean rule form an exact finite-\(n\) minimax saddle.  The correspondingly embedded published least-favorable prior is an exact Bayes-risk converse.  In particular, if \(\rho_{n,2}=\rho_n((1,-1))\), then
\[
 \rho_n(c)=C_0(c)\rho_{n,2},
 \qquad
 d_n(c)=C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]

Second, for arbitrary support, the independent \(q^\star\) design and the explicit clipped-shrinkage estimator in the universal second-order rate theorem satisfy, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 \max_z R_n(\mathcal D^\star,\widehat\tau_n^{\mathrm{sh}};z)
 \leq C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\kappa_c n^{-4/3}\},
 \qquad \kappa_c>0,
\]
where \(\kappa_c\) is the explicit constant in that theorem.  Together with the embedded two-arm converse, this gives
\[
 0<C_0(c)\kappa_c
 \leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{4/3}d_n(c)
 \leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}n^{4/3}d_n(c)
 \leq C_0(c)C_A.
\]

Third, choose rational nonzero zero-sum contrasts \(c^{(n)}\in\mathbb Q^K\) with \(c^{(n)}\to c\), put
\[
 \eta_n=\frac{L_{c-c^{(n)}}}{2},
\]
and choose integers \(M_n\geq1\).  Let
\[
 B_n=B_{n,c^{(n)}}(\nu_{n,M_n,c^{(n)}}),
 \qquad
 U_n=U_{n,M_n}(c^{(n)})
\]
be the exact rational prior and procedure certificates, and define
\[
 R_n^-=\left\{\max(0,\sqrt{B_n}-\eta_n)\right\}^2,
 \qquad
 R_n^+=(\sqrt{U_n}+\eta_n)^2.
\]
Then
\[
 R_n^-\leq\rho_n(c)\leq R_n^+.
\]
The projected rational-certificate procedure has worst-case risk at most \(R_n^+\), while the transferred rational prior certifies the lower bound \(R_n^-\).  If
\[
 \underline d_n=\frac{C_0(c)}n-R_n^+,
 \qquad
 \overline d_n=\frac{C_0(c)}n-R_n^-,
\]
then
\[
 \underline d_n\leq d_n(c)\leq\overline d_n
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 0\leq\overline d_n-\underline d_n
 &=R_n^+-R_n^-\\
 &\leq\frac{5C_0(c^{(n)})}{4M_n^2}
 +4\sqrt{C_0(c^{(n)})}\,\eta_n n^{-1/2}
 +3\eta_n^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
One may choose the approximants so that \(\eta_n=o(n^{-5/6})\); with \(M_n=n\), the displayed improvement bracket then has width \(o(n^{-4/3})\).  If \(c\) is rational, one may take \(c^{(n)}=c\), and the direct exact-rational specialization with \(M_n=n\) has risk-certificate gap at most \(C_0(c)/(4n^2)\).

For \(c=c^\dagger\), one has \(C_0(c^\dagger)=1\), and the direct three-arm certificates satisfy, for every \(n,M\geq1\),
\[
 B_n(\nu_{n,M})\leq\rho_n(c^\dagger)\leq U_{n,M}
 \leq B_n(\nu_{n,M})+\frac1{4M^2}.
\]
The available exact rational calculations through \(n=5\) are the computed three-arm showcase for this formula; they are not used to infer a cross-\(n\) limit.

These conclusions establish exact analytic attainment for two active arms, explicit order attainment for every fixed number of active arms, and scale-matched computable procedure and converse certificates for every real zero-sum contrast, directly exact-rational when the contrast is rational.  They do not determine, when \(|S_c|\geq3\), convergence or the sharp constant of \(n^{4/3}d_n(c)\), sharp second-order optimality of \(q^\star\), convergence of the finite-program optimizers or priors, an analytic limiting feedback rule, or a limiting Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman, spectral, separable, or other operator.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Write
\[
 \alpha=\frac{L_c}{2}=\sqrt{C_0(c)}.
\]
Because \(c\) is nonzero and has zero sum, \(L_c>0\), so \(\alpha>0\).

Suppose first that \(|S_c|=2\).  The zero-sum condition forces the two active coefficients, after relabeling, to be \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\).  Hence the frozen contrast-weighted allocation obeys
\[
 q_a^\star=\frac{|c_a|}{L_c}=1/2
\]
on each active arm.  The published two-arm attainment lemma supplies balanced independent assignment, the posterior-mean estimator, and a least-favorable prior forming an exact finite-\(n\) saddle for contrast \((1,-1)\).  Multiplying the target and estimator by \(\alpha\) multiplies squared loss by \(\alpha^2=C_0(c)\).  The reverse reduction in the embedded two-arm converse supplies the admissible lifted \(K\)-arm procedure, and its forward reduction supplies the matching lower bound.  Therefore
\[
 \rho_n(c)=C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}.
\]
The same forward reduction maps every \(K\)-arm procedure to a binary procedure whose squared loss is no larger than the original loss divided by \(\alpha^2\), schedule by schedule.  Averaging this inequality under the embedded published least-favorable prior gives Bayes risk at least \(C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}\), so that prior is an exact unrestricted-design converse.  The cited Airy expansion gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_n(c)
 &=C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\rho_{n,2}\}\\
 &=C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Inactive arms require no positivity: their coefficients vanish, and neither the lifted target nor the lifted design uses them.

Now allow arbitrary support.  The universal second-order rate theorem constructs the independent \(q^\star\) design and its explicit clipped-shrinkage estimator as an observed-data map into the target interval.  It proves, uniformly over all complete fixed response schedules and for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 \max_zR_n(\mathcal D^\star,\widehat\tau_n^{\mathrm{sh}};z)
 \leq C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\kappa_cn^{-4/3}\},
 \qquad \kappa_c>0.
\]
Using this procedure in the minimax infimum yields
\[
 d_n(c)\geq C_0(c)\kappa_cn^{-4/3}.
\]
The embedded two-arm converse, which permits arbitrary dependent assignments and arbitrary possibly biased estimators, gives
\[
 d_n(c)\leq C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
Multiplication by \(n^{4/3}\) and passage to the lower and upper limits proves the displayed second-order bracket.  For the explicit procedure, \(q_a^\star>0\) on every active arm, so each inverse probability is defined; zero-coefficient arms may have zero probability.  The maximum over schedules still includes the all-zero type, the all-one type, and every face and corner response type.

We next prove the all-real certificate branch.  Let \(c^{(n)}\), \(M_n\), \(\eta_n\), \(B_n\), \(U_n\), \(R_n^-\), and \(R_n^+\) be as in the statement.  The real-contrast grid-certificate transfer theorem applies because each \(c^{(n)}\) is rational, nonzero, and zero-sum, and because \(c^{(n)}\to c\).  It gives directly
\[
 R_n^-\leq\rho_n(c)\leq R_n^+.
\]
Its upper construction uses the rational finite-program design and projects the barycenter rule onto \([-L_c/2,L_c/2]\); therefore it certifies worst-case risk at most \(R_n^+\), without asserting equality.  Its lower construction transfers the same rational response-count prior and gives Bayes risk at least \(R_n^-\) against every design and estimator.

Subtracting the risk bracket from \(C_0(c)/n\) reverses its inequalities.  With the endpoint definitions in the statement,
\[
 \underline d_n=\frac{C_0(c)}n-R_n^+
 \leq\frac{C_0(c)}n-\rho_n(c)
 \leq\frac{C_0(c)}n-R_n^-=\overline d_n.
\]
The endpoint width is exactly
\[
 \overline d_n-\underline d_n=R_n^+-R_n^-.
\]
The quantitative part of the same transfer theorem now yields
\[
 0\leq R_n^+-R_n^-
 \leq\frac{5C_0(c^{(n)})}{4M_n^2}
 +4\sqrt{C_0(c^{(n)})}\,\eta_n n^{-1/2}
 +3\eta_n^2,
\]
which is the claimed displayed bound.

The transfer theorem also constructs rational zero-sum approximants satisfying \(\eta_n=o(n^{-5/6})\).  Since \(c^{(n)}\to c\), one has \(C_0(c^{(n)})\to C_0(c)\), so these constants are bounded.  Taking \(M_n=n\), the three terms in the last display obey
\[
 O(n^{-2})=o(n^{-4/3}),
 \qquad
 o(n^{-5/6})n^{-1/2}=o(n^{-4/3}),
 \qquad
 o(n^{-5/3})=o(n^{-4/3}),
\]
respectively.  Thus the improvement bracket has width \(o(n^{-4/3})\).  If \(c\) is rational, take \(c^{(n)}=c\), so \(\eta_n=0\).  The rational certificate theorem then gives, with \(M_n=n\),
\[
 0\leq U_{n,n}(c)-B_{n,c}(\nu_{n,n,c})
 \leq\frac{C_0(c)}{4n^2}.
\]
This is a direct exact-rational risk-certificate gap rather than an approximation in the contrast.

Finally, set \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\).  Then \(c^\dagger\) is rational, \(L_{c^\dagger}=2\), and \(C_0(c^\dagger)=1\).  The three-arm certificate specialization identifies the general rational certificates with \(U_{n,M}\) and \(B_n(\nu_{n,M})\), and hence, for every \(n,M\geq1\),
\[
 B_n(\nu_{n,M})\leq\rho_n(c^\dagger)\leq U_{n,M}
 \leq B_n(\nu_{n,M})+\frac1{4M^2}.
\]
Thus the existing exact calculations through \(n=5\) instantiate the general theorem but do not enter any passage between population sizes.  Every certificate assertion above is a same-\(n\) risk bracket.  It therefore proves neither convergence of normalized values nor convergence of designs, estimator rules, or priors, and it supplies no analytic limiting operator.  This proves exactly the stated conclusions and exclusions. \(\square\)

They further prove \(\rho_n(c)=n^{-1}-C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), with \(C_A=1.617\ldots\).

For \(K=3\), \(c=c^\dagger\), and integers \(n,M\geq1\), let \((\pi^{n,M},w^{n,M},\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger)\) be an exact rational optimal primal certificate for the grid-action program, and let \(\nu_{n,M}\in\Delta(\mathcal M_{n,3})\) be the response-count multiplier in a complete exact rational optimal dual certificate.  For \(\pi_r^{n,M}>0\), define
\[
 \kappa_{r,x}^{n,M}(g)=\frac{w_{r,x,g}^{n,M}}{\pi_r^{n,M}},
 \qquad
 \delta_{n,M}(r,x)=\sum_{g\in\Gamma_M}g\kappa_{r,x}^{n,M}(g),
\]
and put \(\delta_{n,M}(r,x)=0\) when \(\pi_r^{n,M}=0\).  Define the computable upper certificate
\[
 U_{n,M}=\max_{m\in\mathcal M_{n,3}}
 \sum_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,3}}\pi_r^{n,M}\sum_xP_m(x\mid r)
 \{\delta_{n,M}(r,x)-\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)\}^2.
\]
For any rational prior \(\nu\in\Delta(\mathcal M_{n,3})\), put
\[
 D_{r,x}(\nu)=\sum_m\nu_mP_m(x\mid r),
 \qquad
 N_{r,x}(\nu)=\sum_m\nu_mP_m(x\mid r)\tau_{c^\dagger}(m),
\]
and define the computable lower certificate
\[
 B_n(\nu)=\min_{r\in\mathcal R_{n,3}}
 \left[
 \sum_m\nu_m\tau_{c^\dagger}(m)^2-
 \sum_{x:D_{r,x}(\nu)>0}\frac{N_{r,x}(\nu)^2}{D_{r,x}(\nu)}
 \right].
\]
Then
\[
 B_n(\nu_{n,M})\leq\rho_n^\dagger\leq U_{n,M}
 \leq\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger
 \leq B_n(\nu_{n,M})+\frac{1}{4M^2}.
\]
The upper procedure first draws \(r\) from \(\pi^{n,M}\), assigns uniformly conditional on \(r\), and reports \(\delta_{n,M}(r,x)\); the lower certificate uses the unrestricted posterior mean \(N_{r,x}(\nu)/D_{r,x}(\nu)\), with zero-denominator observations omitted.  Consequently, for any positive normalizer \(a_n\) and integers \(M_n\) satisfying \(a_n/M_n^2\to0\),
\[
 a_n\{U_{n,M_n}-B_n(\nu_{n,M_n})\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
If \(a_nd_n(c^\dagger)\) has a finite limit, both certificate improvements converge to that same limit.  This theorem supplies a finite-\(n\) multivariate rule and an unrestricted rational-prior converse at every such selected normalization; it does not select the normalization, decide whether the independent \(q^\star\) design is second-order optimal, or produce an analytic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman feedback formula.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
The contrast \(c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\) is rational, \(L_{c^\dagger}=2\), \(h_{c^\dagger}=1\), and \(C_0(c^\dagger)=1\).  Therefore
\[
 \Gamma_{M,c^\dagger}=\{-1+j/M:j=0,\ldots,2M\}=\Gamma_M.
\]
After substituting \(K=3\) and \(c=c^\dagger\), the constraints in \(\mathrm{def:rational\text{-}contrast\text{-}grid\text{-}lp}\) are term-for-term the constraints in \(\mathrm{def:k3\text{-}rational\text{-}lp}\).  Hence
\[
 \Lambda_{n,M}(c^\dagger)=\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger.
\]
The exact rational primal and dual certificates whose existence is also established in \(\mathrm{prop:k3\text{-}lp\text{-}certificate}\) may consequently be chosen as the specialization of the certificates in \(\mathrm{thm:rational\text{-}contrast\text{-}grid\text{-}certificate\text{-}sandwich}\).  Under the same substitution, its quantities \(\kappa_{r,x}^{n,M,c}\), \(\delta_{n,M,c}\), \(U_{n,M}(c)\), \(D_{r,x,c}\), \(N_{r,x,c}\), and \(B_{n,c}\) become exactly the quantities displayed in the present statement.  Its finite-sample sandwich therefore becomes
\[
 B_n(\nu_{n,M})\leq\rho_n^\dagger\leq U_{n,M}
 \leq\Lambda_{n,M}^\dagger
 \leq B_n(\nu_{n,M})+\frac1{4M^2}.
\]
All support qualifications also specialize unchanged: divisions by \(\pi_r^{n,M}\) occur only for positive coordinates, zero posterior denominators are omitted, and every \(m\in\mathcal M_{n,3}\), including the all-zero and all-one response types, remains a risk constraint.

For any \(M_n\) with \(a_n/M_n^2\to0\), the specialized certificate gap is at most \(a_n/(4M_n^2)\), proving the displayed convergence.  Moreover,
\[
 a_n\{n^{-1}-U_{n,M_n}\}
 \leq a_nd_n(c^\dagger)
 \leq a_n\{n^{-1}-B_n(\nu_{n,M_n})\},
\]
and the extreme terms differ by a quantity tending to zero.  If the middle sequence converges, squeezing proves that both certificate improvements have the same limit.  The proof uses only same-\(n\) finite programs, so it entails none of the optimizer-convergence, sharp-constant, second-order design-optimality, or analytic-feedback conclusions expressly excluded by the theorem. \(\square\)

For \(K=3\), \(c=c^\dagger=(1,-1/2,-1/2)\), and independent assignment with \(q^\star=(1/2,1/4,1/4)\), define
\[
 Z_i=\operatorname{sign}(c_{A_i}^\dagger)(2Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1),
 \qquad
 \mu_i=t_{i,1}-\frac{t_{i,2}+t_{i,3}}{2}.
\]
Then \(Z_i\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 \mathbb E(Z_i\mid t_i)=\mu_i,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(Z_i\mid t_i)=1-\mu_i^2,
\]
and
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[\left\{\frac1n\sum_iZ_i-\tau_{c^\dagger}(z)\right\}^2\middle|z\right]
 =\frac1n-\frac1{n^2}\sum_i\mu_i^2.
\]
The exact scalar minimax value at \(n=3\), when only \((Z_1,Z_2,Z_3)\) is retained and each \(\mu_i\) ranges over \(\{-1,-1/2,0,1/2,1\}\), is
\[
 V_3^Z=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Nevertheless, an explicit deterministic rule based on the full observed arm labels and outcomes under the same independent \(q^\star\) design has maximum risk
\[
 \frac{511653}{4000000}<\frac{18213}{136000}<V_3^Z.
\]
Thus the map from the full data to \((Z_i)_{i=1}^3\) is not minimax-preserving, even at the fixed \(q^\star\) design, and cannot itself be an exact scalar reduction of the unrestricted three-arm orbit game.  In addition, if \(M_\mu=\sum_i\mu_i\) and \(Q_\mu=\sum_i\mu_i^2\), then over feasible half-integer \(M_\mu\),
\[
 \min Q_\mu=
 \begin{cases}
 |M_\mu|/2,&|M_\mu|\leq n/2,\\
 (3|M_\mu|-n)/2,&n/2\leq|M_\mu|\leq n.
 \end{cases}
\]
Hence the coefficient \(\tfrac12|x|\) is the correct local wedge for the scalar relaxation, but this proposition does not establish that the discarded arm-label information is negligible at any second-order scale.
statements.proof_tex:
Under the stated allocation,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E(Z_i\mid t_i)
 &=\frac12(2t_{i,1}-1)-\frac14(2t_{i,2}-1)-\frac14(2t_{i,3}-1)\\
 &=t_{i,1}-\frac{t_{i,2}+t_{i,3}}2=\mu_i.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Because \(Z_i^2=1\), its conditional variance is \(1-\mu_i^2\).  The assignments are independent across units, and \(n^{-1}\sum_i\mu_i=\tau_{c^\dagger}(z)\), so summing the variances proves the mean-squared-error identity.

We next solve the three-observation scalar game exactly.  Let \(N_+=\sum_{i=1}^3\mathbf1\{Z_i=1\}\), \(M_\mu=\sum_i\mu_i\), and \(Q_\mu=\sum_i\mu_i^2\).  Put
\[
 \alpha=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{6},
 \qquad \delta_Z=\alpha(2N_+-3).
\]
Since \(2N_+-3=\sum_iZ_i\), independence and the preceding moment identities give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\left\{\delta_Z-\frac{M_\mu}{3}\right\}^2
 &=\alpha^2(3-Q_\mu)+(\alpha-1/3)^2M_\mu^2\\
 &=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{18}\{9-3Q_\mu+M_\mu^2\}\\
 &\leq\frac{2-\sqrt3}{2}=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},
 \end{aligned}
\]
where the last step is Cauchy--Schwarz, \(M_\mu^2\leq3Q_\mu\).

For the reverse inequality, put prior weights
\[
 a=\frac{-11+7\sqrt3}{12},\qquad
 b=\frac{8-4\sqrt3}{3},\qquad
 c=\frac{-5+3\sqrt3}{2}
\]
on the five homogeneous mean vectors \((-1,-1,-1)\), \((-1/2,-1/2,-1/2)\), \((0,0,0)\), \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\), and \((1,1,1)\), with respective weights \(a,b,c,b,a\).  These numbers are positive and sum to one.  Direct binomial expansion shows that the observation probabilities \(D_k\), numerator moments \(N_k\), and posterior means for \(N_+=k\) are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 k&D_k&N_k&N_k/D_k\\ \hline
 0&(-1+3\sqrt3)/16&(6-5\sqrt3)/16&-3\alpha\\
 1&(9-3\sqrt3)/16&(-6+3\sqrt3)/16&-\alpha\\
 2&(9-3\sqrt3)/16&(6-3\sqrt3)/16&\alpha\\
 3&(-1+3\sqrt3)/16&(-6+5\sqrt3)/16&3\alpha.
 \end{array}
\]
Thus \(\delta_Z\) is the posterior mean under this prior.  Completing the square gives its Bayes risk
\[
 \sum_jw_j\mu_j^2-\sum_{k=0}^3\frac{N_k^2}{D_k}
 =1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Maximum risk dominates Bayes risk, so the upper and lower bounds coincide and prove the formula for \(V_3^Z\).

We now give the promised full-data witness.  Define
\[
 r_1=\sum_i\mathbf1\{A_i=1\},\qquad
 s_1=\sum_{i:A_i=1}(2Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-1),\qquad
 s_-=\sum_{i:A_i\in\{2,3\}}(1-2Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}).
\]
Let \(1000\delta_F(r_1,s_1,s_-)\) be the following integer table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\qquad}c|r}
(0,0,-3)&-623&(0,0,-1)&-183\\
(0,0,1)&183&(0,0,3)&623\\
(1,-1,-2)&-638&(1,-1,0)&-199\\
(1,-1,2)&148&(1,1,-2)&-148\\
(1,1,0)&199&(1,1,2)&638\\
(2,-2,-1)&-648&(2,-2,1)&-210\\
(2,0,-1)&-167&(2,0,1)&167\\
(2,2,-1)&210&(2,2,1)&648\\
(3,-3,0)&-660&(3,-1,0)&-167\\
(3,1,0)&167&(3,3,0)&660.
\end{array}
\]
This table is exhaustive: for \(0\leq r\leq3\), the compatible values are \(s\in\{-r,-r+2,\ldots,r\}\) and \(h\in\{-(3-r),-(3-r)+2,\ldots,3-r\}\), giving twenty triples.

Here is an exact finite certificate for its risk.  For a response type \(t\), define the Laurent polynomial
\[
 F_t(U,V,W)=\frac12UV^{2t_1-1}
 +\frac14W^{1-2t_2}+\frac14W^{1-2t_3}.
\]
For an orbit \(m\in\mathcal M_{3,3}\), the coefficient of \(U^rV^sW^h\) in \(\prod_tF_t(U,V,W)^{m_t}\) is exactly the probability of \((r_1,s_1,s_-)=(r,s,h)\).  Therefore every risk is the explicitly evaluable rational number
\[
 R_m=\sum_{r,s,h}[U^rV^sW^h]\prod_tF_t^{m_t}
 \left\{\delta_F(r,s,h)-\frac13\sum_tm_t
 \left(t_1-\frac{t_2+t_3}{2}\right)\right\}^2.
\]
Expanding the eight factors for the \(\binom{10}{7}=120\) response-count orbits and comparing integer numerators after clearing the common denominator gives
\[
 R_m\leq\frac{511653}{4000000}.
\]
Equality holds exactly at the count vectors \((1,0,0,0,0,0,0,2)\) and \((2,0,0,0,0,0,0,1)\), in lexicographic type order \(000,001,010,011,100,101,110,111\).  As a direct boundary check, for the schedule \((000,111,111)\), whose target is zero, the six nonzero orbit probabilities give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R&=\frac18(183/1000)^2+\frac18(638/1000)^2
 +\frac14(199/1000)^2+\frac14(167/1000)^2\\
 &\quad+\frac18(648/1000)^2+\frac18(167/1000)^2
 =\frac{511653}{4000000}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For a fully rational scalar lower certificate, use weights \((1/10,7/20,1/10,7/20,1/10)\) on the same five homogeneous scalar states.  Their observation masses are \((17,15,15,17)/64\), their numerator moments are \((-219,-63,63,219)/1280\), and their prior second moment is \(3/8\).  Completing the square gives
\[
 \frac38-\sum_{k=0}^3\frac{N_k^2}{D_k}
 =\frac{18213}{136000}>\frac{13}{100}
 >\frac{511653}{4000000}.
\]
The strict gap proves the asserted failure of minimax preservation without floating-point arithmetic.

Finally, each feasible scalar mean belongs to \(\{-1,-1/2,0,1/2,1\}\).  Pointwise,
\[
 \mu^2\geq\frac{|\mu|}{2},
 \qquad
 \mu^2\geq\frac{3|\mu|-1}{2}.
\]
Summing and using \(\sum_i|\mu_i|\geq|M_\mu|\) gives the two lower branches for \(Q_\mu\).  If \(|M_\mu|\leq n/2\), equality is obtained by using \(2|M_\mu|\) entries equal to \(\operatorname{sign}(M_\mu)/2\) and all remaining entries zero.  If \(|M_\mu|\geq n/2\), equality is obtained with \(2|M_\mu|-n\) entries equal to \(\operatorname{sign}(M_\mu)\) and the remaining entries equal to \(\operatorname{sign}(M_\mu)/2\).  This proves the wedge formula, including its face junction at \(|M_\mu|=n/2\).

For every integer \(n\geq1\), every \(K\geq2\), and every nonzero zero-sum contrast \(c\), write \(\rho_{n,2}=\rho_n((1,-1))\) for the unrestricted two-arm minimax risk with the same population size. Then
\[
 \rho_n(c)\geq C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}.
\]
If \(|S_c|=2\), this inequality is an equality. Moreover,
\[
 0\leq d_n(c)\leq C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\rho_{n,2}\}
 =C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
When \(|S_c|=2\), the upper bound in the last display is also an equality, so \(d_n(c)=C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\rho_{n,2}\}\). The finite-sample lower bound permits arbitrary dependent assignment designs and arbitrary possibly biased estimators.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Put
\[
 P_c=\{a:c_a>0\},\qquad N_c=\{a:c_a<0\},\qquad I_c=\{a:c_a=0\}.
\]
Because \(c\) is nonzero and \(\sum_a c_a=0\), both \(P_c\) and \(N_c\) are nonempty and
\[
 \alpha:=\sum_{a\in P_c}c_a=-\sum_{a\in N_c}c_a
 =\frac12\sum_a|c_a|=\frac{L_c}{2}>0.
\]
In particular, division by \(\alpha\) below is lawful and \(\alpha^2=C_0(c)\).

\textbf{The embedded two-arm experiment.}
Let \(y=((y_i^+,y_i^-))_{i=1}^n\in\{0,1\}^{2n}\) be an arbitrary binary two-arm response schedule, where \(+\) and \(-\) denote the two arm labels. Embed it into the \(K\)-arm schedule \(E_c(y)\) by
\[
 t_{i,a}=y_i^+\quad(a\in P_c),\qquad
 t_{i,a}=y_i^-\quad(a\in N_c),\qquad
 t_{i,a}=0\quad(a\in I_c).
\]
Writing \(\tau_2(y)=n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i^+-y_i^-)\), the zero-sum identity gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_c(E_c(y))
 &=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
 \left(\sum_{a\in P_c}c_a y_i^+
       +\sum_{a\in N_c}c_a y_i^-\right)\\
 &=\alpha\,\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i^+-y_i^-)
 =\alpha\tau_2(y).
 \end{aligned}
\]

Fix any legitimate \(K\)-arm procedure \((\mathcal D,f)\). To construct a legitimate two-arm procedure, first draw a latent \(A\sim\mathcal D\), independently of \(y\). Set the binary assignment \(B_i=+\) when \(A_i\in P_c\), set \(B_i=-\) when \(A_i\in N_c\), and, when \(A_i\in I_c\), draw \(B_i\) by a fair coin independent of everything else. This induces a probability law on \(B\in\{+,-\}^n\) that is fixed before the response schedule is revealed, so it is an admissible two-arm design. Let \(v_i=y_i^{B_i}\) be the observed binary outcome and define the pseudo-observation supplied to \(f\) by
\[
 \widetilde v_i(A,B,v)=
 \begin{cases}
 v_i,&A_i\in P_c\cup N_c,\\
 0,&A_i\in I_c.
 \end{cases}
\]
For the embedded schedule, \((A_i,\widetilde v_i)_{i=1}^n\) is exactly the data seen by the original \(K\)-arm procedure: active-arm outcomes agree because \(B_i\) is the sign group of \(A_i\), and inactive-arm outcomes were fixed at zero.

The latent scaled action \(H=\alpha^{-1}f((A_i,\widetilde v_i)_{i=1}^n)\) need not be a function of the observed binary data, because it retains \(A\). Remove this hidden information by defining, for every binary observation \((b,v)\) having positive design probability,
\[
 g(b,v)=\mathbb E\!\left[H\mid B=b,\,(y_i^{B_i})_{i=1}^n=v\right],
\]
and define \(g\) arbitrarily in \([-1,1]\) on zero-probability observations. This is a schedule-independent function of \((b,v)\): conditional on \(B=b\), the latent law of \(A\) is determined entirely by \(\mathcal D\) and the inactive-arm coins, while \(v\) is a deterministic function of \((b,y)\) and supplies no further restriction on \(A\). Equivalently, \(g(b,v)\) is obtained by averaging \(\alpha^{-1}f(A,\widetilde v(A,b,v))\) under the known conditional kernel \(\Pr(A\in\cdot\mid B=b)\). Since \(f\in[-L_c/2,L_c/2]=[-\alpha,\alpha]\), one has \(g\in[-1,1]\), as required for the two-arm estimator action space.

Conditional Jensen's inequality and the embedded-target identity now yield, for every binary schedule \(y\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_y\{g(B,v)-\tau_2(y)\}^2
 &\leq \mathbb E_y\{H-\tau_2(y)\}^2\\
 &=\alpha^{-2}
 R_n(\mathcal D,f;E_c(y)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Taking the maximum over \(y\), then using that \(E_c(y)\) ranges over a subset of the \(K\)-arm schedules, gives
\[
 \rho_{n,2}
 \leq\alpha^{-2}\max_z R_n(\mathcal D,f;z).
\]
The original \((\mathcal D,f)\) was arbitrary. Taking its infimum proves
\[
 \rho_n(c)\geq\alpha^2\rho_{n,2}=C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}.
\]
This argument explicitly handles assignments to inactive arms: their binary outcomes are lawfully generated under the induced design and then discarded, while the original procedure receives only the fixed zero specified by the embedded schedule. No outcome unavailable under the two-arm assignment is used.

\textbf{Reverse reduction for two active coefficients.}
Suppose \(|S_c|=2\). The zero-sum condition implies that the two active coefficients are \(c_{a_+}=\alpha\) and \(c_{a_-}=-\alpha\). Given any two-arm procedure \((\mathcal D_2,f_2)\), define a \(K\)-arm design by mapping every binary assignment \(+\) to \(a_+\) and every binary assignment \(-\) to \(a_-\); inactive arms receive probability zero. Report \(\alpha f_2\). For every \(K\)-arm schedule \(z\), the induced binary schedule is \(y_i^+=t_{i,a_+}\), \(y_i^-=t_{i,a_-}\), and therefore
\[
 \tau_c(z)=\alpha\tau_2(y),
 \qquad
 R_n(\mathcal D_K,\alpha f_2;z)
 =\alpha^2R_{n,2}(\mathcal D_2,f_2;y).
\]
Taking worst cases and then the infimum over two-arm procedures gives
\(\rho_n(c)\leq\alpha^2\rho_{n,2}\). Together with the embedded lower bound,
\[
 \rho_n(c)=C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}\qquad\text{when }|S_c|=2.
\]
No positivity condition is needed for inactive arms because neither the target nor the lifted design uses them.

\textbf{Universal first-order upper bound and the second-order ceiling.}
Under the frozen contrast-weighted independent design, \(q_a^\star=|c_a|/L_c>0\) for every \(a\in S_c\). Before projection, write the estimator as \(n^{-1}\sum_i W_i\), where
\[
 W_i=\sum_{a\in S_c}
 \frac{c_a\mathbf 1\{A_i=a\}}{q_a^\star}
 \left(t_{i,a}-\frac12\right).
\]
The zero-sum condition implies
\[
 \mathbb E(W_i\mid z)
 =\sum_{a\in S_c}c_a\left(t_{i,a}-\frac12\right)
 =\sum_a c_at_{i,a}.
\]
Moreover, \(c_a/q_a^\star=L_c\operatorname{sign}(c_a)\) on \(S_c\), and binary outcomes give \((t_{i,a}-1/2)^2=1/4\). Hence
\[
 \mathbb E(W_i^2\mid z)=\frac{L_c^2}{4},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(W_i\mid z)\leq\frac{L_c^2}{4}.
\]
The assignments are independent across units, so the unprojected rule is unbiased for \(\tau_c(z)\) and has risk at most
\[
 \frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(W_i\mid z)
 \leq\frac{L_c^2}{4n}=\frac{C_0(c)}n.
\]
Since every \(\tau_c(z)\in[-L_c/2,L_c/2]\), projection onto that interval cannot increase squared loss. Therefore \(\rho_n(c)\leq C_0(c)/n\). Combining this upper bound with the embedded converse gives
\[
 0\leq d_n(c)=\frac{C_0(c)}n-\rho_n(c)
 \leq C_0(c)\{n^{-1}-\rho_{n,2}\}.
\]
The cited two-arm theorem gives
\(n^{-1}-\rho_{n,2}=C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3})\), so, for fixed \(c\),
\[
 0\leq d_n(c)
 \leq C_0(c)C_A n^{-4/3}+o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
When \(|S_c|=2\), the exact equality for \(\rho_n(c)\) makes the upper bound an equality. This also checks the boundary schedules with all embedded outcomes zero or all one: they remain legal schedules, the target identity still holds, and the simulation reveals no unavailable potential outcome. \(\square\)
